author: Collider
title: Goodfellas Opening Scene Proves Martin Scorsese's Gangster Genius | Entertainment
text:
Martin Scorsese's Goodfellas opening scene, with Ray Liotta's iconic gangster line, defines the film's tragic story of Henry Hill and organized crime.
Martin Scorsese's Goodfellas, released in 1990, remains one of the most celebrated gangster films ever made, and its opening scene stands as a defining moment in cinema. Set in New York City from the 1950s through the 1980s, the film follows Henry Hill, played by Ray Liotta, as he rises and falls within one of the city's Mafia families. More than three decades after its premiere, the movie's influence on the gangster genre endures.
Scorsese Redefines Gangster Cinema
Few directors have explored organized crime with the depth and style of Martin Scorsese. From early works like Mean Streets to later films such as The Departed and The Irishman, he has spent decades examining the criminal underworld. His films create compelling characters, both real and fictional, while avoiding simple glorification.
Goodfellas is often considered his magnum opus. Its staying power comes from unforgettable performances, a legendary soundtrack, and Scorsese's precise direction. The film captures both the allure and the brutality of Mafia life without romanticizing it.
Unlike Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather, which opens by suggesting the Mafia can help those seeking justice, Goodfellas wastes no time showing that gangsters are out for themselves alone. That difference defines Scorsese's approach to the genre.
The Opening Line That Defines Henry Hill
The film begins with Henry, Jimmy Conway, and Tommy DeVito driving down a dark highway. They hear noises from the trunk and pull over. Inside is a badly wounded gangster named Billy Batts, played by the late Frank Vincent.
What follows is a shocking act of violence. Tommy stabs Billy before Jimmy finishes the job with a gunshot. As Henry closes the trunk, Ray Liotta delivers the film's famous opening line: As far back as I can remember, I always wanted to be a gangster. Tony Bennett's Rags to Riches begins to play.
In just 13 words, Scorsese establishes the thesis of his masterpiece. The line introduces a man whose fascination with organized crime will ultimately be his undoing. It also highlights the disconnect between Henry's romanticized view of the Mafia and its horrifying reality.
Henry Hill's Tragic Downfall
After the violent opening, the film jumps back to Henry's childhood. He admires the men he sees every day because they represent money, power, respect, and freedom from society's laws. His desire to become a gangster shapes his entire life.
Goodfellas follows Henry as he works with Jimmy Conway, played by Robert De Niro, and Tommy DeVito, played by Joe Pesci. He rises within the Mafia but eventually sees friends die and is swallowed by the life. He betrays those closest to him and enters the witness protection program, a fate most mobsters consider the ultimate betrayal.
The final narration reveals how deeply organized crime has shaped Henry's worldview. Instead of expressing remorse, he doubles down. His only regret is losing the luxury he enjoyed. His greatest punishment is being forced to live as an ordinary person.
Henry laments that everything is different, that there is no action, and that he has to wait around like everyone else. He complains about getting egg noodles and ketchup instead of spaghetti with marinara sauce. He calls himself an average nobody who will live the rest of his life like a schnook.
That conclusion perfectly answers the promise of the opening scene. Henry spends his entire life chasing an idealized version of organized crime, only to discover the lifestyle is unsustainable. Goodfellas remains a masterclass in showing why the gangster dream is a dangerous myth.
